speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance if they can give me any information as to the truth of a statement appearing in this morning's paper to the effect that after the first of April next empire goods in order to obtain free entry into Great Britain must have a fifty per cent empire content in labour and materials. Is that correct?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EMPIRE CONTENT OF GOODS ENTITLED TO PREFERENCE IN GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext: At the sessions of the Imperial economic conference which took place at Ottawa, the discussion as to empire content was carried forward for some time and various suggestions were made. Generally speaking, fifty per cent was regarded as a reasonable empire content, and the British government concluded from their standpoint that they would fix fifty per cent, effective from the first of April next, as sufficient empire content to entitle goods to the benefit of the empire preference. That refers, however, not t,o all goods, but to a limited number, particulars of which I shall in due course lay on the table of the house. The report in the press is a summary of what the intention of Great Britain is. We finally agreed at the time of the conference that each country could probably best decide for itself what would be a reasonable content, and the matter will be further considered at the meeting of the committee on cooperation which will be convened on the fourteenth of February.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED EXCHANGE OF CANADIAN CATTLE AND OTHER COMMODITIES FOR PETROLEUM AND OIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some question has
been raised regarding trade relations with Russia, and I thought that at this time it would be well to make a statement as far as possible covering the whole field.
1.	A trade agreement was negotiated in 1921 between the United Kingdom and the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics. On August 22, 1921, and December 26, 1921, through appropriate minutes in council, the government of the United Kingdom were informed that Canada desired to participate in the arrangement, and a formula to be embodied in notes to be exchanged between the British foreign office and the Russian trade delegation with the object of making applicable to Canada the provisions of the trade agreement was approved by the Canadian government. Effect was given to this decision by an exchange of notes, under date of July 3, 1922, and the British trade agreement was applied to Canada from that date. Subsequently a Russian trade delegation was established in Canada.
2.	A general treaty of commerce was negotiated in 1924 between the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics and the British government, but in November, 1924, after the Labour party was defeated in the general election, the new Foreign secretary, Mr. (now Sir) Austen Chamberlain, indicated to the Russian representative that the government found themselves unable to recommend the treaty in question to the consideration of parliament or to submit it to the King for His Majesty's ratification, so. that Anglo-Russian commercial relations continued to be governed bv the trade agreement of 1921.
3.	Following like action by the United Kingdom, Canada formally recognized the Soviet government by letter from Mr. King, the then Prime Minister, dated March, 24, 1924, directed to Mr. A. Yazikoff, the Soviet official agent at Montreal.
4.	In May, 1927, a search was made of the offices of the Anglo-Russian trade organization in London and as a result the trade agreement between Russia and Great Britain was terminated. The Russian representatives were requested to leave the country on the ground that as the result of the search it was conclusively proved that military espionage and subversive activities throughout the British empire were directed and carried on from the offices of the organization. The

Russian Mission denied the statements but complied with the request to leave Great Britain, and the British representative in Moscow was simultaneously withdrawn. Canada took the same position as the United Kingdom. Mr. King, then Prime Minister announced that Canada had taken independent action and declared itself free from the obligations of the agreement, and he further stated that this action was being taken "on our own initiative as a result of the evidence we have before us at the present time" as well as on "the statement of the British Prime Minister in parliament", which "leaves no doubt as to propaganda being conducted by the agents of the Soviet". In the note sent by Mr. King to the Soviet official agent in Canada, he informed him that the Canadian government had concluded that the Soviet authorities had failed to "refrain from hostile action or undertakings and from conducting outside their own borders any official propaganda direct or indirect against the institutions of the British empire, which was an essential condition of the agreement as entered into by Canada as well as by the United Kingdom".
5.	On April 16, 1930, a temporally commercial agreement was entered into between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom |ad. the government of the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics pending the conclusion of a formal treaty of commerce and navigation. The agreement was to remain in force until a commercial treaty was concluded subject, however,^ to the right of either party at any time to give notice ^ to the other to terminate the agreement, which remained in force until the expiration of six months from the date on which such notice was given. The protocol contained a provision that the contracting parties were animated by the intention to eliminate from their economic relations all forms of discrimination, and that they agreed that, so far as relates to the treatment accorded by each party to the trade with the other, they would be guided in regard to the purchase and sale of goods, in regard to the employment of shipping and in regard to all similar matters by commercial and financial considerations only and, subject to such considerations, would adopt no legislative or administrative action of such a nature as to place the goods, shipping, trading organizations and trade in general of the other party in any respect in a position of inferiority as compared with the goods, shipping and trading 'organizations of any other foreign country.
6.	In 1930 by chapter 3 of the statutes of that year parliament conferred upon the gov-

Trade Relations with Russia
ernor in council power to place an embargo against goods imported from any country which was not a party to the treaty of Versailles.
On February 27 and December 10, 1931, pursuant to the powers thus conferred, orders in council were passed, the effect of which was to prohibit the importation of coal, wood-pulp, pulpwood, lumber and timber of all kinds, asbestos and dressed furs from the Soviet Union.
At the Imperial conference in August, 1932 a trade agreement was entered into between the United Kingdom and Canada. Article 21 of which reads as follows:
This agreement is made on the express condition that, if either government is satisfied that any preferences hereby granted in respect of any particular class of commodities are likely to be frustrated in whole or in part by reason of the creation or maintenanced directly or indirectly of prices for such class of commodities through state action on the part of any foreign country, that government hereby declared that it will exercise the powers which it now has or will hereafter take to prohibit the entry from such foreign country directly or indirectly of such commodities into its country for such time as may be necessary to make effective and to maintain the preferences hereby granted by it.
Having regard to the provisions of the temporary trade agreement entered into by the United Kingdom with the Soviet Republics in 1930, as above mentioned, effect could not be given bo article XXI so long as that trade agreement continued in force. In consequence of this, the British government on October 17, 1932, notified the Soviet government of the termination of the agreement, which would thus be terminated six months from that date, or on the seventeenth day of April, 1933. The British government a.t the same time intimated their willingness to open negotiations with the Russians for a new agreement. It was not suggested at any time during the discussions at the Imperial conference that Great Britain should cease to trade with Russia. On the contrary, the British representatives made it perfectly clear at all times that trading operations on a large scale had been carried on and that credits had been established which, in point of fact-, were renewed shortly after the conclusion of the Ottawa conference. Similarly, except for the articles covered by the embargo there have never been any restrictions on trading between Canada and Russia, except that in 1931 Russia placed an embargo against the importation of any commodities from Canada.
Later in 1932 a private arrangement was made between an aluminum company in Canada and the Soviet government, under which a certain quantity of aluminum was purchased and paid for by petroleum. The government of Canada was not a party to the transaction except in so far as it became necessary to determine the duty payable on the imported petroleum.
It may be of interest to the Manchester Guardian and other British papers which have been so vigorously assailing the government during the last few weeks that, in consequence of the embargo against the importation of Russian coal, employment has been afforded to Welsh and Scotch miners to the extent necessary to produce for importation into Canada during the calendar year 1932, 1,399,086 tons of anthracite coal.
While returning to Canada from Great Britain, in December last, I received press messages by wireless that an agreement had been concluded between Canada and Russia for the exchange of Canadian cattle, hides, and other commodities for Russian petroleum and coal. I replied that there was no foundation for such reports. No communication of any kind has been received from the Soviet government in this regard.
It would appear that one G. G. Serkau, with associates, conceived the idea of doing a barter business with Russia, and Mr. Serkau, having seen Mr. Weir, the Minister of Agriculture, at Ottawa, proceeded to New York and later to Moscow in connection with the business. As a matter of fact he went there apparently as the emissary of a syndicate, the expenses being provided by one well-known member of it. Although he alleges that he had communication with the authorities there, he has produced no evidence that he has any agreement with the Soviet government, and no communication regarding his proposals have been received from them. The mere statement of what the proposals of Mr. Serkau are would be sufficient to indicate that this is an effort to make very substantial profits under circumstances to which I shall presently refer.
On December 21 last, Mr. Serkau wrote Mr. Weir, the Minister of Agriculture, as follows:
Since we aim to obtain for the Canadian cattle producers at least five eente for grade, and a much higher price for registered stock, the total amount payable by the Russian government for 100,000 head of oafetle, including freight, etc., will be in the neighbourhood of $8,000,000. On the other hand, the prices at Black sea ports of the commodities that Russia is to give in return are so low that it will require an enormous tonnage of petroleum products, etc.
Having in mind the time required for marketing and storage facilities in Canada, I

Trade Relations with Russia
am of the opinion that there will be substantia! balances owing to our corporation from time to time, unless, of course, we are to renew negotiations with Russia for a much slower delivery of the cattle, say over a period of two or two and a half years instead of twelve months. This, however, I fear, will militate against our chances of producing the desired effect, i.e., to increase the price of cattle in Canada. Moreover, particularly in the case of western grade stock, you will appreciate that during the months of July to November, we will have to lift enormous numbers of cattle.
I believe that my associates and myself, with what capital we could muster and with expected assistance from banks or other sources, could finance the purchase of a cargo or two of c-attle, including the freight and expenses to Black sea ports. This, I estimate, would be about $1,000,000. Therefore, if we could take Sufficient quantities of kerosene, lubricating oil and anthracite we could probably get along without any financial support from your government. Or, if we spread the deliveries of cattle over a period of two or two and a half years, as I said before, we may be able to market the products received in payment as we deliver the stock.
But I am firmly convinced that it will be necessary for us to ship the live stock within the twelve month period, in fact, perhaps deliveries would almost have to be completed by November of 1933 if we are to serve the interests of the Canadian live stock producers. I expect also that it would be unsafe to estimate that we could handle the enormous tonnage of petroleum, etc., within that period.
Therefore, I think it would be wise to figure on a basis of your government guaranteeing Russian seven per cent bonds payable June 1, 1935, for such balances as may be owing to our corporation from time to time. The total amount involved in such guarantees I would estimate at not more than $4,000,000, at any time and only very little of these bonds will remain unpaid at the end of the term, for the reason that we will be taking deliveries continuously and the value of such deliveries *null be applied on the bonds.
In asking for this support from the government, our corporation would be prepared to employ the government's nominee as comptroller of disbursements and receipts.
1 learned abroad that the German government established a credit to Russia of $75,000,000 and cashed Russian bonds at par as these bonds were received by German exporters and presented to the treasury. The British government guaranteed Russian bonds received by British exporters to the extent of sixty per cent. This partial guarantee satisfied the British exporters owing to the fact that they increased their prices to Russia to such an extent that sixty per cent paid them for their merchandise, pins reasonable profits. Our case is somewhat different inasmuch as the increase in prices of live stock from the present market price of two and one-quarter cents to five cents per pound, will enure to the benefit of the producers and not to our corporation. Therefore, it will be necessary for us to have balances fully guaranteed.
It should be observed that the nature of this transaction is largely in the interests of the live stock industry, the profits to myself and my associates being merely brokerage commission.
IMr. Bennett.]
One other form of support that I imagine we will require is some manner of protection against breach of contract by the Russian government. While we will under no circumstances make any disbursements until the contract has been signed on behalf of tile Russian government and until a representative of that government has arrived in Canada and approved of live stock purchases, still I fear that careful bankers, under present conditions, will demand some manner of assurance that our corporation will incur no loss if the Russian government should fail to accept the cargoes of stock, or tail to deliver the products to be given in payment. This, of course, could, at the most, only involve a cargo or two of live stock, and I do not believe that there is the slightest chance of default by the Russian government, but I do expect to be confronted with that question when applying for assistance from banks even for short term financing.
Accompanying the communication was a memorandum of suggested conditions of trade transactions between the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics and the Canadian syndicate, represented by Mr. Serkau; but there is no evidence that the Soviet government or its representatives ever agreed to these proposed suggestions, and on being pressed Mr. Serkau had to admit that they were merely notes of suggestions that he himself made. The memorandum reads as follows:
Suggested conditions of a trade transaction between the U.S.S.R., hereinafter referred to as the " Union," and
The Canadian syndicate, represented by G. G. Serkau, hereinafter referred to as the " Syndicate."
The union to purchase from the syndicate
100.000 live cattle (to include five per cent pedigreed and registered stock) within a period of one year from the date of the contract. The stock to be purchased by the syndicate from Canadian producers in the presence of inspectors of the union.
The price of live stock to be cost plus cost of purchasing, maintenance, freight, insurance, etc., plus one cent per pound.
That is the brokerage. It only runs between twenty and thirty per cent!
The syndicate to deliver the live stock to Black sea ports and to receive at Black sea ports credits to be given by the union on account of payment for the stock purchase.
To apply on payment for the stock so purchased the union is to deliver to the syndicate f.o.b. Black sea ports the following products in quantities as hereinafter stated:
Petrol:	During the months of April to
October, 1933, both inclusive, 2,000 metric tons per month.
During the months of November 1933, to March i934, both inclusive, 5,000 metric tons per month, and
From April 1931, to the end of the term,
20.000	metric tons per month.

5.000	to 15,000 metric tons per month during the term.
Lubricating Gil: Beginning with April 1933, from 200 to i,000 metric tons per month during the term.

April 1933, from 3,000 metric tons to 20,000 metric tons per month during the term.
In the above, in every ease where the tonnage is in varying quantities per month, such variations shall be at the option of the syndicate.
The syndicate to have the privilege of buying from the union, pulpwood for delivery in the United States of America, and shall apply the value of such pulpwood purchases on account of payment of the live stock sold to the union. The prices of all the products to be delivered by the union in payment of stock purchases herein to be, in the case of petroleum products prevailing	universal or	basis	current Gulfprices, and for anthracite the price to be not in excess	of	the prices	paid	by Canadianimporters	of	anthracite	coal	from Britishexporters. Balances owing by the union to the syndicate from time to time shall be subject to interest at seven per cent per annum, such interest charges to commence on the dates of advances made by the syndicate with respect to purchase of live stock or expense advances, and the union to be credited with the value of its deliveries of products as above, on the days when such products have been loaded into ships for shipment into Canada.
The reply of the minister to this communication and memorandum was to request that he be given such information as would satisfy him that any agreement existed between Mr. Serkau and his associates and the Soviet union. This information has not yet been supplied. The letter reads as follows:
Ottawa, December 23, 1932.
G. G. Serkau, Esq.,
Chateau Laurier,
Ottawa, Onit.
Dear Mr. Serkau:
I would refer you to the subject matter of our discussions on various occasions since the 15th October, and particularly since your return from Russia, with regard to the purchase in Canada of 100,000 head of cattle for export to Russia, in exchange for petroleum products etc., from that country to Canada.
I would be glad to place before my colleagues the proposed transaction as outlined in the memorandum which you submitted upon receipt of a definite statement from you that the government of the U.S.S.R. is desirous of entering into trade on such a basis as you outlined.
Yours very truly,
R. Weir.
No further communications have been received in that regard.
I think this house will agree that no Canadian government would seriously consider a proposal to provide credit facilities for a syndicate of vendors and at the same time to guarantee -that the alleged purchaser, the Soviet government, would discharge its obligations to the vendors.
Shortly put, the matter stands in this light. Proposals were made on behalf of promoters
desirous of entering into a commercial transaction for profit. The proposals are in writing. They contemplate the payment by the purchasers of commission of from 20 to 30 per cent depending upon the value of the live stock, the commission being one cent per pound. A request was made that a guarantee be given not only for one half of the entire suggested purchase price, namely $4,000,000, but also that the government of Canada should guarantee that the government of Russia would keep its alleged undertakings with those who put them forward. That is the proposal.
The minister, before even submitting it to the government for consideration, asked for evidence of the bona fides of the transactions. It has not yet been received and those who are interested in the propaganda that has been carried on in this country by at least two public newspapers, and the manner in which it has been carried on, will be able to decide for themselves whether or not despatches, sometimes carrying a date line of a community in which they were not written, to arouse, on the strength of statements that were made in the public press or elsewhere, we do not know, anticipations which were incapable of realization, are conducive under present conditions to the national welfare.

speechtext:
Perhaps the
minister would give us a brief explanation of the bill. It is some time since we have had an opportunity of considering it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Sections 1, 2, 3 and 4 are
designed to amend the law relating to personal corporations. I shall have the statute here in a moment or two, but it will be remembered that the income tax law creating personal corporations was enacted in 1926. This law was made applicable to personal corporations as then described existing in 1925 and thereafter. Prior to that time the law had been that a company paid a company tax and the individual shareholders paid a tax only as and when dividends were declared. Realizing that the company tax was but 9 per cent-I am speaking now as of that time-and the individual tax by successive brackets of income rose as high as 40 per cent on incomes up to $140,000 and higher in the higher brackets if an individual had an income above that sum, many individuals resident in Canada were incorporating companies which they controlled, the income of which was not a manufacturing or merchandising one, but was income derived from stocks, bonds, debentures, real estate, such as dividends, interest, rent and so forth. This income was taxed at corporation rates of taxation and higher bracket rates were avoided. The personal corporation section, in effect, for taxation purposes ignored the existence of the company and continued to tax the individual on the income of the company as if the individual had received it direct, and thus brought the income by brackets for taxation purposes under the increasing rates of taxation. As regards the date 1917, that strikes one as a long time to go back. The reason 1917 is inserted is, as I am sure the hon. member knows, there was provision in the income tax law that profits which were not distributed could be computed prior to the end of 1917 and paid out without tax. After that, these profits were taxable. That is the reason for the insertion of 1917. If someone in juggling with his tax liabalities has done so relying upon the special legislation that appeared in the act with relation to profits to the end of 1917, I say that he as well as anybody else who has not paid the correct amount should

be called upon to pay. It has been said that there shoidd be a period of limitation. Frankly, I do not believe one man should be allowed to say: Well, time ran against me and I got out of paying what was honestly my fair payment under the law, while another man comes along and says: They picked me up because they got me within two or three years as suggested. I think an honest debt should be paid and the debt the taxpayer owes is an honest one. Exactly what it is can be found. If it takes some time to find this out, that is unfortunate and I agree with the hon. member for North Waterloo that it is not in the interest of good business, if that were the test; but, as I am sure he knows, auditors of the department over which he presided had to go from 1930 back to 1923 or 1924 and when it was found mistakes had been made, as obviously was the case, the findings of the auditors of course being carefully checked, money was requested to liquidate the debt. All that was said was: You have been concerned about this for a long time; but no real objection could be taken to paying what was the honest liability of the taxpayer. I think section 8 could very well pass. It will result in legitimate help to the taxpayer and I think it will help the tax collecting authorities.

In the
section as now drafted there is nothing that gives a taxpayer the right to use it. Further, the draftsman, when he drew this and made the explanation, to be found on the opposite page, had in mind only re-assessment on the part of the crown. I am not against the crown getting its just and legitimate revenue; I think any member who would take any other view would be doing a great wrong not only to the country but to his self respect. But I ask respectfully that there should be some limitation of time. Let me put an extreme case. Under the New Brunswick Succession Duties Act there is a provision that every gift inter vivos by a testator to his children or to anybody has to be accounted for back to the year 1892, the first year in which the New Brunswick Succession Duties Act was passed. It is almost impossible to get a client to take the oath under the New Brunswick Succession Duties Act that there has not been anything like that done, because you cannot have knowledge going back forty-one years. That is the effect of the New Brunswick statute. I mention that as an extreme illustration, and the analogy is applicable here. I suggest to the minister that he give some consideration to a shortening of the time. I will not press the point further.

Income War Tax Act

I regret that I find it
necessary to differ from the views expressed by the Minister of National Revenue as to the interpretation of this section. If it ever was intended that the section should confer any benefit on the taxpayer, then I can only say that it is one of the most loosely-drawn pieces of legislation I have ever seen. Read the section and see what it says:
-the minister may at any time assess, reassess or make additional assessments upon any person for tax, interest and penalties.
How on earth can he be assessing, re-assessing or making additional assessments for tax, interest or penalties if the object is to make some refund to the taxpayer in respect of the application of the tax? I am not shedding any crocodile tears, but I think we might as well keep one thing clearly in mind. If the object of this section is to get at any person who has not made a return or who has made a false return, then I will go as far as any member of this house in making that person pay taxation. But that is not the point. If a man were wise, as I believe the Minister of Finance said, he would get a certificate; but let us assume that he is not so very wise but honest. There are any number of executors and trustees who are not lawyers. I can go through my files and find cases in which I have settled income tax matters with the income tax department and have never yet received a certificate, nor do I expect ever to receive it. The point in which we are interested in this section is this. Where a man honestly but inadvertently, and, if you will, unwisely, makes a return which ultimately proves to be incorrect, should the minister have power after the expiration of sixteen years, by a combination of that section with section 10, to go back and make an assessment particularly in such a case as the one pointed out by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, where the individual has been acting as trustee for an estate and has probably had all the funds disbursed out of his hands? My whole training makes me unalterably opposed to retroactive legislation, and in this case it goes a bit further and I think we may work a great injustice. If the object of the legislation is to get at a wrongdoer who has failed to make a return or who has made a false return, why not say so?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I do not wish to prolong the argument, but I would direct attention to the wording of the section, which I think the lay mind can interpret:
-the minister may at any time assess, reassess or make additional assessments upon any person for tax, interest and penalties.
That. I submit, does not mean that he can make a re-assessment only in case the amount is larger than what has been returned. If the department were approached in an honest case the minister would be authorized undeT this section to make a re-assessment, and when I say a re-assessment I mean a true reassessment, which might very well be in the interests of the taxpayer.
I would call attention to section 56, which covers the point of refund of overpayment. This section we are discussing cannot mean what the minister suggests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the section is a reasonable one. I do not think we should be led astray by interpreting it in connection with section 10. I have already agreed to let section 10 stand. I submit, with all deference, that we are not asking for any further powers than the act has contained; it is only for the purpose of making it clear beyond perad-venture and avoiding any question of dispute such as has arisen heretofore in individual cases.
If section 8 were redrafted, section 10 which we are allowing to stand might not be necessary at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is substantially what has always been contained in the act. Look at section 62:
Upon receipt of the said notice of dissatisfaction and statement of facts, the minister shall reply thereto by registered post admitting or denying the facts alleged and confirming or amending the assessment or any amended, additional or subsequent assessment.
We have always had these provisions. As regards the section which is now before us, it may not be drafted in the best possible manner, and I am open to suggestions on that score; but I can say at all events that its intention is to clarify the law as it has obtained heretofore in this matter. There certainly cannot be any objection to it in principle, and I do not think we should be led astray by interpreting it in connection with the retroactive features contained in section 10, which we are permitting to stand for the moment for further consideration at the request of my hon. friend from Stanstead.

Why is
this necessary?
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can give an explanation, in layman's language, I hope. In the statutes of 1930, chapter 24, we did what I must submit was a very extraordinary thing. Section 19 provides:
On the winding-up, discontinuance or reorganization of the business of any incorporated company, the distribution in any form of the property of the company shall be deemed to be the payment of a dividend to the extent that the company has on hand undistributed income earned in the taxation period 1930 and subsequent periods.
That meant opening the door to a glorious opportunity on the part of a great many companies to go out of business and distribute accumulated profits, calling them assets, thus escaping taxation, so that the treasury lost many hundreds of thousands of dollars in consequence of that amendment. Some companies, in the guise of distributing assets, did this in effect: A company would cause a new company to be incorporated; it would transfer the assets to individuals who in turn handed them over to the new company in exchange for redeemable certificates, and from time to time these redeemable certificates were cashed by the new company; and inasmuch as they were capital they were not taxable. It was certainly a very grave injustice to a large number of companies who were, and had been for years, distributing their income. The position is that companies which went through that process merely for the purpose of escaping taxation, as and when those individuals cash in the stock certificates, shall be taxed four per cent. That is fair to the individual; the tax on the average is lower than it would be if it had been assessed upon the income throughout the year. I will admit that there is an element of retroactivity, but, on the other hand, I believe it is equitable, sound and just.

I support entirely the action of the minister in making this amendment to the legislation passed in 1930. Strangely enough, at that time the possible unfortunate consequences of this legislation escaped the jbservation of the lawyers in the house, to say nothing of the laymen, and were not realized until some clever lawyers in the pay of corporations and others discovered this loophole and reincorporations were made with a view to escaping the tax. So far as I am personally concerned it was mortifying and humiliating to find that such a loophole had been left, and I am quite in agreement with what the minister is doing to eliminate it. I may add that if a loophole was left in the first instance it was not by any means intentional.
When a company is insolvent and the assets are distributed, can those assets be taxed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section would have
no bearing whatsoever upon such a case.

On section 10-Application of sections.

Earlier in the session
I asked the Minister of Finance if he intended to provide for the taxing of bearer bonds. Rightly or wrongly I understood him then to say that at this session he would bring in an amendment to the Income War Tax Act making such a provision. I cannot find anything to this effect in the bill. Is the minister taking any action to see that the holders of bearer bonds pay their rightful share of income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not customary to
anticipate what will be contained in the budget, but I feel that in this case an exception is justified, especially in view of the intimation made at an earlier stage of the session. I can assure my hon. friend that legislative provision will be made at this session which will fully protect the treasury in respect of those who have hitherto escaped taxation in the matter of bearer bonds. For many months I have studied the various systems and methods which could be applied, and I think we have devised a scheme which will be simple, effective, and not unduly irksome in the way of unnecessary impedimenta so far as the individual is concerned. This will have the effect of bringing into the treasury every last cent of money which ought to come from those who have bearer bonds.

I am taking advantage of
the fact that we are in committee to ask the minister a question regarding a case which came to my notice a few days ago. A gentleman moved to Canada from the United States; for three months of the tax year he was in Canada and for nine months he had resided in the United States. He tells me that he was compelled to pay the Canadian authorities income tax upon his full year's income, while he paid tax to the United States upon the income he had earned during the part of the year he was in that country. It seems to me that an injustice has been done. Will the minister inform me whether or not that is the correct procedure under the present act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not the minister
responsible for the administration of this act, but. I am advised by the income tax authori-

Incow,e War Tax Act
ties that the tax payable in such cases is determined by the facts as to place of residence at the time a resident is subject to income tax. That being so, there is no method of deviating from' the taxation in question. In the example given by my hon. friend, while the individual would be called upon to pay his income tax in Canada by virtue of his being resident in Canada at a time when residents of Canada were liable to income taxation, since he had been assessed in the United States he would be able to ask for and obtain in Canada an allowance for such portion of income tax as he had paid in the United States. The opposite applies, also, as this is a matter of international comity which has I believe worked out very satisfactorily.

When I asked the minister
the question I had forgotten that the act was not under his administration; perhaps I should have directed my question at another time to the Minister of National Revenue. I understand from this man that the department would not make him an allowance on account of his having had to pay an income tax to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am assured by the commissioner of income tax that the statement which I made to my hon. friend is correct- that where the source of income has been in the United States the taxpayer can claim and receive a deduction in Canada for that portion of his income tax which he paid to the United States.
In view of the fact that many provinces impose income taxes, has this government considered the advisability of collecting these taxes for such provinces and turning over the proceeds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This question was raised
at the recent interprovincial conference While I am not in position to say that any definite decision was reached, I think there was a near approach to a possible amicable solution which will meet the cases mentioned by my hon. friend.
Section stands.
On section 4-Shareholders to file statement of personal corporation.

I do not know whether
or not I am in order, but if I am I should like to make a serious suggestion to the government in connection with our judges. The judges' salaries have been reduced, and in view of this fact I think the government should consider the providing of proper accommodation. At the present time the
supreme court is sitting in what was previously a shed used by the contractors for the construction of the old parliament buildings as a shelter and storehouse. These quarters are very unsuitable for the judges, and if the government has seen fit to reduce their salaries I think it should follow the example set by the United States, which country is now constructing a new supreme court building in Washington. It would give our supreme court decent quarters, and would at the same time provide work for the unemployed. Our supreme court judges have to sit in a room where the temperature is often eighty degrees and then go back to their offices where the temperature may be down to sixty, with a great risk of catching cold. The building is not a fit place for the Supreme Court of Canada. I suggest that the government provide fitting accommodation for the court and at the same time do something in a practical way for the unemployed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Temis-couata, with his usual versatility and ingenuity, has succeeded in hanging a very large garment upon a very small peg; for under the guise of a discussion of the Income Tax Act, he has discussed the income tax on judges' salaries, ergo the building that houses the judges-
Because their salaries are small, their accommodation at least should be decent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must commend my hon friend upon his ingenuity, groat versatility and resourcefulness, which are always in evidence. While I cannot see what bearing his remarks have upon this bill, I agree with him that the question not only of proper quarters for the accommodation of the members of the supreme court itself, but also of the preservation against fire hazards of a very valuable library, is one which is worthy of very careful consideration by this parliament, and I hope that the day is not far distant when the objection my hon. friend has raised may possibly be met.
Thank you very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend from Quebec South mind repeating the objection which he raised to section 4?

I have referred to the definition of a "personal corporation'' as laid down in section 1 of this bill. The definition reads:
"Personal corporation" means a corporation or joint stock company, irrespective of when or where created, whether in Canada or else-

where, and irrespective of where it carries on its business or where its assets are situate, controlled, directly or indirectly, by one individual who resides in Canada, or by one such individual and his wife or any member of his family, or by any combination of them or by any other person or corporation or any combination of them-
Taking that to be the definition of a personal corporation, I now turn to section 4, subsection 7 of this bill, which reads:
The shareholder of a personal corporation who controls such corporation shall file with his income tax return a statement of the assets, liabilities and income of the personal corporation.
I ask the minister what would happen if the shareholders were a combination of several who controlled. My hon. friend from Stanstead shakes his head.
It is not a personal corporation under the definition and is not entitled to the immunities that go with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Quebec South will find that the definition clause includes "shareholders" as well as "shareholder, the plural as well as the singular.

I have in mind,, for instance, one individual and a corporation who control a personal corporation. Would this individual and the corporation also be bound to file an income tax return of the assets and liabilities and income of the personal corporation? I take it from the wording of subsection 7 that they would not, because that subsection states that it is the shareholder who controls who must file the return. That would be only one shareholder. It might be that a combination is in control.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the interpretation clause, that would be read in the plural- shareholder or shareholders or any combination of them.

I do not wish to persist if the minister is satisfied, but the same argument that he applied to section 8 would apply here. The reason why we make section 8 more severe is that some taxpayer was led into error by certain phraseology in section 8. I submit that taxpayers would certainly be led into error by the phraseology of subsection 7 of section 4, and now, while we are making the act clear, we might as well make it clear in all its sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not feel that I am competent to enter into a legal discussion as to the proper construction of this section-
My hon. friend is now sarcastic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I am not in any sense attempting to be sarcastic. I am speaking in all seriousness, because it is about twenty-five years since I have had any contact with the law. I am advised by the income tax authorities that they are satisfied, after a conference with the legal advisers of the crown in the Department of Justice, that there is no danger as far as the interpretation of this section is concerned.
